tagline: Two river valleys meet a narrow forest crossing and covered bridges.
intro: The Myrtle Creek–Canyonville Tour Route links farmland, streams and forest in the southern Cascade foothills east of I-5. Oregon's Department of Transportation highlights those contrasts in its Tour Route description and gives 68 miles and three to four hours. Parts are gravel or single lane, including the steep, narrow approach to Red Top Pond. Forest Road 2810 passes through old-growth Douglas fir, with openings toward the Rogue-Umpqua Divide Wilderness. On the South Umpqua leg, the route passes historic homes and produce farms; on South Myrtle Creek, the hills hold cattle and sheep.

The route's bridges record changes in local travel. At Milo, a 1920 wooden covered bridge became inadequate for the academy's heavy farm vehicles. A steel replacement arrived in 1962, with the old covering adapted to fit it. At Myrtle Creek, timbers from Lane County's former Horse Creek Bridge were reused for a crossing to Mill Site Park.

Traveling from Myrtle Creek toward Canyonville, follow South Myrtle Creek into the hills to Red Top Pond. The forest crossing leads to South Umpqua Road and Tiller. Follow the South Umpqua west past Milo and Days Creek to Canyonville.

moments.title: Myrtle Creek
moments.text: Timbers from a bridge in another county became a crossing to Myrtle Creek's Mill Site Park. The original Horse Creek Bridge was built in Lane County in 1930. A concrete bridge bypassed it in 1968; it served pedestrians before being dismantled. Some of its timbers went into a small covered bridge in Cottage Grove, and others came here. The reused wood now spans Myrtle Creek between a parking area and the park. The creek itself forms where North Myrtle Creek and South Myrtle Creek join, then flows into the South Umpqua.

moments.title: Red Top Pond
moments.text: Red Top Pond sits at the change between the South Myrtle Creek road and the steep forest crossing. The reservoir is a fishing and picnic destination on BLM Road 28-3-35. Beyond it toward Tiller, the route uses Forest Roads 2792 and 2810. Douglas fir forest along 2810 opens occasionally toward the Rogue-Umpqua Divide Wilderness.

moments.title: Milo Academy Bridge
moments.text: The wooden housing at Milo covers a steel truss. The original wooden bridge dated from 1920, but by 1962 the academy considered it unsafe for the heavy farm vehicles used in its agriculture program. The replacement steel bridge initially had no covering. Residents wanted to keep the familiar covered form, so the old covering was adapted to the new structure. Four rectangular windows line each side above the South Umpqua River. Milo Adventist Academy owns and maintains the bridge. The 100-foot, single-lane span has vertical wood siding and a gabled roof clad in metal.
moments.notice: Four rectangular windows line each side of the wooden housing.

practical: Red Top Pond: The steep, narrow one-lane road can be hazardous for motor homes and trailers and is often closed in winter. (checked 2026-10-11)
